events.text: Every typhoon season the fishing village of Seven Shoals rings a bronze bell at the harbour mouth, three slow strokes and one quick, to tell you a storm is coming and their boats are out. For two hundred years the rhythm has never changed. This year the old ringer has died, and a girl of twelve is ringing it like a cook beating eggs.

choices.text: Answer the bell anyway, and turn the storm

effects.log: You come up the coast in the rain and lean on the storm until it bends north. The boats come home. The girl on the pier rings the bell again, wildly, all wrong, and you find you like it.

choices.text: Wait for the proper rhythm

effects.log: You wait for three slow and one quick. It never comes. Two boats are late home, and the village says the dragon has grown proud.

choices.text: Rise beside the pier and hum it for her

effects.log: You rise beside the pier with rain running off your horns and hum it: three slow, one quick. She drops the mallet, picks it up, and gets it right on the fourth try.

events.text: The bell-ringer of Seven Shoals is grown now, and has added something. After the three slow strokes and the quick one come two very soft ones. Nobody in the village knows what they mean. When you come up through the harbour mist the ringer calls across the water that they mean thank you, in advance.

choices.text: Accept the new rhythm

effects.log: You learn the two soft strokes the way you learned the first four. From then on you come a little faster to them than to the rest.

choices.text: Ask for the old rhythm to be kept for strangers

effects.log: The ringer agrees: the old rhythm for the boats of other villages, the new one for Seven Shoals. You can tell the two coasts apart in the dark now.

choices.text: Ring the bell once yourself, with your tail

effects.log: The bell is very loud. The pier is somewhat damaged. The village tells the story for a century and never once repairs that plank.

events.text: The old ringer's grandson rings the bell now, and the bell has cracked at last. The village wants to recast it with one of your scales in the bronze, so that you will always know its voice, whoever rings it.

choices.text: Give them a scale

effects.log: You shed one on the beach at low tide, the size of a door. The new bell has a green sheen and a voice you would hear at the bottom of the sea.

choices.text: Tell them to keep the cracked bell

effects.log: A cracked bell has a voice like nothing else on the coast. You would know it anywhere, and so, it turns out, would every boat.

choices.text: Tell them to listen to the sea instead

effects.log: You tell the grandson what the sea sounds like a day before a storm. The village learns it in a generation, and rings the bell only for you.

events.text: A scale you shed in a river long ago has turned up in a county apothecary's window, on red silk, under a sign that says it cures fever, baldness and bad luck. A queue of the sick runs round the block. The scale, you notice from the river, is not even yours. It is a carp's, painted.
events.arc: The Scale in the Apothecary Window

choices.text: Shed a real one on the apothecary's step

effects.log: In the morning there is a scale on the step the size of a tray, still wet. The apothecary faints, wakes, and takes the painted one out of the window.

choices.text: Send the apothecary a dream

effects.log: The apothecary dreams all night of a vast eye at the window. In the morning the painted scale is gone, and so is the sign.

choices.text: Leave it: the queue is comforted

effects.log: Half the queue feel better anyway. You decide not to try to understand this.

events.text: Your real scale works. Not on baldness, but on fever: water poured over it comes off cold and sweet, and the summer fever in the county breaks in a month. Now the provincial governor wants the scale sent to the capital, where the fevers are worse.
events.arc: The Scale in the Apothecary Window

choices.text: Let it go to the capital

effects.log: The scale goes north in a lacquered box with an escort of twenty. The county is sad about it, and then proud about it, which is the county's way.

choices.text: Shed a second one for the capital

effects.log: You shed another, more slowly. Both fevers break. You are sore along the flank for a season and do not mind.

choices.text: Rise in the river and ask for it to stay

effects.log: The governor's men see you at the ford and set the box down on the bank, very gently, and back away. The scale stays in the county.

events.text: Generations on, the scale is a temple treasure, and a monk has written a sutra about it. The sutra describes you, with great respect, as a modest serpent of the third rank. Pilgrims rub the silk under the scale bare.
events.arc: The Scale in the Apothecary Window

choices.text: Correct the sutra in a dream

effects.log: You dictate the correction to the monk's successor in a dream. The new copy calls you a modest serpent of the first rank. The monks argue about the word modest for years.

choices.text: Let it stand

effects.log: A modest serpent of the third rank. You turn it over in the deep pool for a decade and decide you like it.

events.text: In the cold mountain spring where you hatched, a small serpent has made its home: finger-thick, furious, and sure it will be a dragon by next summer. It has heard of you. It would like to know how you did it, and also whether it may have the pearl when you are finished with it.
events.arc: The Serpent in Your Old Spring

choices.text: Tell it the truth: a thousand years

effects.log: You tell it about the thousand years. It is silent for a whole day, then asks which year was the worst. You tell it that too.

choices.text: Frighten it into manners

effects.log: You let one eye fill the spring. It hides under a stone for a month and comes out very polite.

choices.text: Show it the pearl, once

effects.log: You open your claw over the spring. The little serpent looks at the pearl for a long time and then asks, much more quietly, what it has to do.

events.text: The little serpent is not little any more. It has a horn bud, a temper, and a village downstream that leaves it rice and complaints. It comes to you at the river mouth to ask what to do about a fisherman who keeps netting its pool.
events.arc: The Serpent in Your Old Spring

choices.text: Tell it to bend the net, not the fisherman

effects.log: It bends the net every night for a year. The fisherman mends it every morning and goes on to tell everyone that the pool is very lucky for practice.

choices.text: Go and speak to the fisherman yourself

effects.log: You speak to the fisherman from the shallows. Afterwards the fisherman fishes elsewhere and leaves rice at both pools, to be safe.

choices.text: Tell it to work it out alone

effects.log: It works it out. The fisherman fishes somewhere else now and says the pool is haunted. The young serpent is proud of this. You are less sure.

events.text: A storm over the Nine Falls, and in it a shape you know: the serpent from your old spring, climbing. It is not ready. You can see it is not ready, and so can the witness on the bank, a woodcutter with his mouth open.
events.arc: The Serpent in Your Old Spring

choices.text: Lift it the last length yourself

effects.log: You take its tail in your claw and lift. It goes over the top of the falls and keeps going. It is not a dragon. It is a serpent who has been higher than it should, and it knows it.

choices.text: Call to the woodcutter: say what you see

effects.log: The woodcutter shouts the first word that comes. It is not dragon. It is snake. The young serpent falls back into the pool, and the woodcutter apologises to both of you all the way home.

choices.text: Let it fall, and catch it in the pool

effects.log: It falls, as you fell once. You catch it before the rocks. It sulks for a decade and then begins again, more slowly, which is the only way.

events.text: On the fifteenth day of the first month the valley flies kites to send off the bad luck of the year, and this year every kite in your Ward is you: blue paper dragons with long tails, two hundred of them, wagging over the paddies. One small one has its whiskers drawn on upside down.
events.arc: The Dragon Kites of the First Month

choices.text: Send a wind to lift them all

effects.log: Two hundred blue dragons climb at once, higher than kites have ever flown. The whole valley cheers. It is very good for your pride.

choices.text: Lift only the crooked one

effects.log: The small crooked kite goes up and up while the fine ones flap at the treetops. The child on the string is speechless, then unbearable.

choices.text: Let the wind do what it likes

effects.log: Half the kites end in the persimmon trees. Nobody blames you. It is a very ordinary wind.

events.text: The kite-flying has become a contest. The village whose kite climbs highest is said to have the dragon's favour for the year, and the two villages on the east bank have stopped speaking over it. The headmen have asked you, through the shrine, to name a winner.
events.arc: The Dragon Kites of the First Month

choices.text: Name neither: the sky is not a prize

effects.log: Your answer comes as a single gust that tangles every kite in the valley together. The two villages spend a day untangling them side by side, and speak again.

choices.text: Name the kite with the crooked whiskers

effects.log: The child who drew the whiskers upside down is from neither village. Both headmen are furious, and then they laugh, and then they copy the whiskers.

choices.text: Name the highest kite

effects.log: The winners are insufferable for a whole year. The losers build a bigger kite. You find you enjoy the contest more than you should.

events.text: Years on, a kite comes up to you in a storm, and not on a string: someone has cut it loose to carry a message. On its paper tail, in a child's hand: The well is dry. Please.
events.arc: The Dragon Kites of the First Month

choices.text: Bring the rain

effects.log: You turn the storm down the valley and empty it on the village with the dry well. The kite comes down with the rain, soaked, and the child keeps it for life.

choices.text: Bring the rain, and keep the kite

effects.log: The rain comes. The kite does not. It stays up in the storm with you for a hundred years, and the village says the dragon keeps letters.

events.text: The county has appointed a clerk to keep a ledger of your rain: every shower, which village, how long. The clerk is very thorough, measures it in thimbles, and has found that the west bank has had more rain than the east for forty years. The east bank has filed a complaint. Against you.

choices.text: Rain more on the east bank

effects.log: You lean the clouds a little east every summer. The east bank withdraws its complaint. The west bank files one.

choices.text: Explain that rain follows the hills, not favour

effects.log: You explain to the clerk in a dream how the ridge lifts the wind. The clerk draws a diagram of it in the ledger, wrong, and very proud of it.

choices.text: Rain on the clerk

effects.log: Only on the clerk. For three days. The ledger records it faithfully, in a wet hand.

events.text: The clerk is old now, and the ledger fills forty volumes. The clerk climbs your ridge with the last one and asks to be allowed to write one thing that has never been written in it: why.

choices.text: Tell the clerk why the rain falls where it falls

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. The clerk writes until the brush is bald and goes down the ridge with the most complete account of rain anyone has ever had.

choices.text: Tell the clerk you do not always know

effects.log: The clerk writes it down very carefully: The dragon does not always know. Then, under it, smaller: Neither do I.

choices.text: Let a single drop fall on the page

effects.log: One drop, exactly in the middle of the last page. The clerk draws a circle round it and labels it: Answer.

events.text: The forty volumes of the rain ledger are found in a county storehouse by a young official who has a drought coming and no idea where to dig the reservoirs. The thimble counts show exactly where the water goes.

choices.text: Show the official where your ridge holds water

effects.log: You let the springs on your flank run high for a week, so that anyone can see. The reservoirs are dug at the foot of them.

choices.text: Let the ledger speak alone

effects.log: The official digs where the clerk's thimbles point. The reservoirs fill. A stone is put up to the clerk, not to you, and you find that right.

choices.text: Rain where the reservoirs will be dug

effects.log: You rain on the right places a season early. The official decides the ledger and the dragon agree, and digs with great confidence.

events.text: The village well where you were laid as an egg on a first full moon is to be filled in. There is a new well now, deep, with a stone wheel, and the old one breeds mosquitoes. An old woman sits on its rim every evening and will not let them shovel.
events.arc: The Well You Were Laid In

choices.text: Let them fill it

effects.log: You let it go. The well is filled on a grey morning and you feel it, a small cold spot on your old self, like a tooth gone.

choices.text: Send clean water up through it once more

effects.log: The water rises to the brim, clear as the night you were laid, and the mosquitoes go elsewhere. The shovels go back in the shed.

choices.text: Speak to the old woman on the rim

effects.log: She tells you she drew water from it the morning after you were laid, saw the glow, and never told anybody. The village leaves the well alone for her.

events.text: The old woman is gone. The children of the village drop wishes into your old well now, on folded paper: for a puppy, for rain, for a brother to come home from the army. The paper softens at the bottom. You can read every one.
events.arc: The Well You Were Laid In

choices.text: Grant the small ones

effects.log: Three puppies are found in three barns that spring. The well becomes very popular.

choices.text: Grant only the rain

effects.log: You grant the rain and leave the puppies to the dogs. The paddies have their best year in a decade.

choices.text: Grant the brother

effects.log: It takes a storm on a road far to the north, and a bridge that is down for exactly one day too long for the army to wait. The brother walks home.

events.text: The well has a little roof now, and a stone that says Dragon Well, and the wishes that came true are carved on the stone in rows. At the bottom someone has carved, very small: and the rest it did not. The village laughs about it every year.
events.arc: The Well You Were Laid In

choices.text: Grant one more, to the carver

effects.log: The carver wished, it turns out, for the carving to be finished before the frost. It is. The carver adds a line: and one more.

choices.text: Leave the joke as it is

effects.log: You leave it. It is the truest line on the stone, and the children learn to read on it.

events.text: One of the ghosts who walk behind you, a thin one in a straw hat, has been coughing politely for a week. When you turn at last, it bows. Its sister is marrying tomorrow in the village where it was born, and it would like a day off. Only a day. It will come straight back.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Asked for a Day

choices.text: Give it the day

effects.log: It goes down the mountain at a run. It comes back at dusk smelling of rice wine and very happy, and walks behind you more lightly than before.

choices.text: Give it the rest of its days

effects.log: You tell it not to come back. It stands very still in the road. Then it goes down to the wedding and stays, and the walking behind you is a little lighter.

choices.text: Refuse: the tiger's ghosts walk with the tiger

effects.log: It bows again and falls back into line. You hear the wedding drums on the wind all next day, and so does it.

events.text: The ghost in the straw hat is back with another request. Its niece has been born, and it would very much like to be there for the hundredth-day feast. It has, it explains, already told the baby all about you.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Asked for a Day

choices.text: Let it go to the feast

effects.log: It goes. It comes back with a bit of rice cake stuck to its hat, which is impossible, and will not explain.

choices.text: Let it go for good this time

effects.log: It goes down to the feast and does not come back. Somewhere in that village a baby grows up with an uncle nobody else can see.

choices.text: Go with it, and wait at the edge of the village

effects.log: The village sees a white tiger sitting at the edge of the barley through the whole feast and decides it is the best omen anyone has had in years.

events.text: Word travels among the dead. The ghosts who still walk behind you have heard about the one in the straw hat, and one morning they line up in the road, holding up small requests written on oak leaves.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Asked for a Day

choices.text: Read every leaf

effects.log: It takes all day. A grave to visit, a debt to forgive, a dog to see once more. You grant what you can, and the line walks behind you afterwards in a different way.

choices.text: Release the oldest of them

effects.log: The oldest one has been with you longest and asked for least. You let it go first. It does not look back, which is how you know it was time.

choices.text: Tell them to walk properly

effects.log: The leaves blow away down the road. The line closes up. The magpie on the pine says nothing, very loudly.

events.text: Every child under your mountain knows the story: a crying baby would not hush for the threat of a tiger, but hushed at once for a dried persimmon, and the tiger at the window fled, sure the persimmon was a monster worse than itself. This winter the children have laid dried persimmons along the ridge path, in a row, to keep you off it.

choices.text: Flee the persimmons, loudly

effects.log: You leap back from the first one with a great show and bound into the pines. The children shriek with joy. The path is theirs now. You go round by the gully.

choices.text: Sit beside the row and wait for them

effects.log: You sit by the persimmons all day like a cat by a mousehole. Nobody comes. By evening the whole village knows the tiger is besieging its own path.

choices.text: Move each persimmon one step down the path every night

effects.log: By the end of winter the row of persimmons has walked itself down to the village gate, and the children are frightened in an entirely new way.

events.text: The persimmons have worked too well. The woodcutters carry them as charms now, and one is coming up your pass at night with a string of them round his neck, singing, straight toward a she-bear with cubs.

choices.text: Step out onto the path in front of him

effects.log: He sees you, stops singing, and sits down very hard. The bear, who has no wish to meet a tiger either, takes her cubs elsewhere.

choices.text: Turn the bear yourself

effects.log: The bear does not want to be turned. It takes some arguing, with claws. The woodcutter sings all the way home and never knows.

choices.text: Let the persimmons do their work

effects.log: The bear smells the string, takes it off him very gently with one paw, and eats every persimmon. The woodcutter tells the village the charms work, only differently.

events.text: The persimmon story has a new ending in the villages now. In it the tiger comes back the next winter and asks the baby, very politely, where one might find such a monster, so as to make friends with it. You have no idea who started it.

choices.text: Make the new ending true

effects.log: At New Year you put your great white head in at a farmhouse window. A child holds out a dried persimmon on a flat palm. You take it as gravely as a seal of office.

choices.text: Roar once from the ridge, to keep the old ending alive

effects.log: The roar comes down the valley like a door slamming. The old ending is back in every house by morning, and so are the persimmons.

events.text: The Autumn Court sits on the bare summit under the western stars, and the first case of the season is a hare. A fox has eaten its whole warren, it says. The fox does not deny it. It only says that foxes eat hares, and that the court of the White Tiger is the last place in the mountains that should pretend otherwise.

choices.text: Pardon the fox: hunger is not a crime

effects.log: The fox bows and goes. The hare sits on the summit until dawn and then goes too, and the court is quiet for a long time after.

choices.text: Punish the fox: a whole warren is greed

effects.log: You send the fox off the mountain for a year and a day. It goes. Every fox in the province learns the difference between a meal and a warren.

choices.text: Sentence the fox to feed the hare's last kits for a year

effects.log: The fox stares at you. The hare stares at you. The court, such as it is, stares at you. The fox goes off with three kits in a row behind it, looking appalled.

events.text: The court is crowded this autumn. Word has got round that the White Tiger hears small cases, and the summit is full of them: a magpie against a squirrel over a pine cone, two toads over a puddle, a very old badger who wishes to complain about the weather.

choices.text: Hear every case

effects.log: It takes the whole autumn. You are hungry by the end of it, and the mountain is very orderly.

choices.text: Hear only the badger

effects.log: The badger's complaint is serious after all: the first frost comes later every year, and the dens are flooding. You send word to the north.

choices.text: Close the court to anything smaller than a deer

effects.log: The small creatures go away grumbling. The court is faster, and grander, and somehow knows less.

events.text: The fox comes back to the summit, grey at the muzzle, followed by three large hares. It fed them a year, and then another, and somewhere in there it stopped being able to eat hares at all. It asks the court what it is supposed to eat now.

choices.text: Let it eat from the mountain god's offerings

effects.log: You give it a place at the edge of the shrine where the rice and fruit are left. It eats like a monk and looks very surprised to be alive.

choices.text: Tell it that it is a fox, and a fox can decide

effects.log: It goes away to decide. You hear later that it eats mice and never once looks at a hare.

choices.text: Take the lot of them into the court

effects.log: The Autumn Court now has a fox usher and three hare clerks. The cases are filed beautifully and nobody is ever eaten on the summit again.

events.text: A young ferryman on your stretch of river has heard the old story about a tortoise who beat a hare, and decided it was about you. Every morning now he poles his ferry alongside your rock and challenges you to race to the far bank. The snake wants to accept. The tortoise is asleep.

choices.text: Let the snake accept

effects.log: The snake says yes in a voice like a hinge. The tortoise wakes halfway across the river, extremely surprised, and you win by a shell.

choices.text: Let the tortoise sleep

effects.log: The ferryman races your rock every morning for a month, alone, and wins every time, and stops in the end out of embarrassment.

choices.text: Let the two heads talk it over

effects.log: The heads talk until noon. By then the ferryman has a passenger, and you race him at the speed of a tortoise and a snake in agreement, which is slow.

events.text: The race has become the river's festival. Every year on the fifth day of the fifth month the ferryman, older and broader, poles out against you, and the banks are lined with people. This year the snake has read an omen in the water: the ferry will founder at midstream, during the race.

choices.text: Lose on purpose, and stay under the ferry

effects.log: You dawdle so badly the banks jeer. At midstream a plank gives, and you are right there under it, and the ferry rides home on your back.

choices.text: Have the snake tell the ferryman

effects.log: The snake tells him, in front of everyone, exactly which plank. He checks. It is rotten through. The race is held a day late, on a new plank.

choices.text: Win, and come back for whoever falls

effects.log: You win by a length and turn back at once. Three passengers are in the water. You bring up all three, and the ferryman, who is laughing too hard to swim.

events.text: The ferryman is very old. The ferry belongs to his granddaughter now, and she has no interest in racing. On his last good day he asks to be poled out to midstream, to your rock, for one more go.

choices.text: Race him slowly, and let him win

effects.log: He wins by a nose and does not believe it for a moment. He thanks the tortoise for its manners and the snake for its patience, which confuses them both.

choices.text: Race him properly

effects.log: He loses by a whole shell and laughs until he coughs. 'At last,' he says. 'An honest race.'

choices.text: Carry him across on your back instead

effects.log: You carry the ferryman over the river he has crossed ten thousand times. He says it looks different from up here, and it does.

events.text: Two scholars from the capital have come with paper, ink pads and a ladder: they want a rubbing of your shell for the Royal Archive. The tortoise is willing to lie still. The snake has noticed that one plate says something about the scholars' own dynasty that the scholars will not like.

choices.text: Lie still, and let them copy it all

effects.log: They ink every plate. The older scholar reads the one about the dynasty twice, rolls the paper very tightly, and says nothing all the way back to the capital.

choices.text: Let the snake smudge the one plate

effects.log: The snake drips river water on the plate at exactly the wrong moment. The rubbing has a grey cloud in one corner. The tortoise is not pleased.

choices.text: Tell them what the plate says before they ink it

effects.log: The older scholar sits on the ladder for a long time. Then inks it anyway. 'An archive that only keeps what it likes is a pantry,' the scholar says.

events.text: The rubbing of your shell is famous now. Copies of copies hang in schoolrooms, and children trace the plates with their fingers to learn the old script. A copyist in the capital has made an error on one plate, and now three hundred schoolrooms teach that your river freezes in summer.

choices.text: Freeze the river one summer morning

effects.log: One morning in the sixth month the river at your ford is a sheet of white ice. It melts by noon. Three hundred schoolrooms are vindicated.

choices.text: Send the correction by the ferry

effects.log: It takes the correction eleven years to reach the capital. The copyist is mortified and very grateful.

choices.text: Leave it: the children like the idea

effects.log: You leave it. The snake says a wrong thing that makes children curious is worth more than a right thing nobody reads. The tortoise lets it win this one.

events.text: The dynasty the plate spoke of has ended, on the day and in the way your shell said. The younger of the two scholars, white-haired now, comes down to your river with the old rubbing under one arm and sits by your rock without a word.

choices.text: Show the scholar the next plate

effects.log: The snake turns the shell so the scholar can see the plate beside it, the one about the dynasty after. The scholar reads it and smiles for the first time.

choices.text: Sit with the scholar until dark

effects.log: Neither of you says anything. When the scholar goes, the rubbing is left on your rock, weighted with a stone, as if returned.

events.text: In the hardest winter of a century the river freezes almost to the bottom at your ford, and in the black ice, a hand down, you find a letter: folded, sealed, three hundred years old, addressed to someone in a village that is now a pine wood. The snake can read where it was meant to end.

choices.text: Carry it where it was meant to go

effects.log: You wait for the thaw with the letter under your chin. The snake says the road ends at the pine wood, and the tortoise sets off.

choices.text: Let the snake open it

effects.log: It is a proposal of marriage, very shy, with a pressed flower. The snake reads it aloud to the tortoise, who is moved, and pretends not to be.

choices.text: Leave it in the ice

effects.log: You leave it. It melts out in the spring and goes downstream, and somewhere, you suppose, it is still on its way.

events.text: At the edge of the pine wood, under a pine split by lightning, two graves lie side by side, unmarked. The snake is sure: the letter's writer and the one it was written to. They were buried together after all, says the snake, and nobody ever told them the letter was lost.

choices.text: Bury the letter between the graves

effects.log: You dig with one forefoot, slowly, and lay the letter in the earth between them. The pine above drops a cone, which the snake says is a reply.

choices.text: Let the snake read it aloud to them both

effects.log: The snake reads it in its best voice, the one it saves for the Dragon King. The tortoise keeps very still the whole time.

choices.text: Keep the letter under your shell

effects.log: You keep it, and carry it back to the river. Some things, the snake says, should be kept by somebody who will not forget them.

events.text: The pine wood is cleared for paddies, and the farmers find the two graves and mean to move them. The snake has read where it ends: one grave to each end of the valley, by two different families who each claim one.

choices.text: Lie down over the graves

effects.log: The farmers find an enormous black tortoise asleep across both graves. They plough round you for a season, and then for good, and the paddies have a little island in them still.

choices.text: Let the snake tell the farmers the story

effects.log: The snake tells it at the headman's gate, letter and all. Both families claim the pair together now, and the graves stay where they are.

choices.text: Let them be moved

effects.log: They are moved. You go to both ends of the valley in turn, the slow way, and tell each one what the other is doing.

events.text: A palace page of nine with ink on every finger has discovered that you know a lie, and has made a game of it. Every morning on the way to lessons the page stops at the gate and tells you one: I ate no breakfast. I can fly. My teacher is kind. Then waits, delighted, to see your horn dip.
events.arc: The Child Who Lies to Your Horn

choices.text: Dip the horn every time

effects.log: Your horn dips for breakfast and for flying. The page laughs all the way to lessons and comes back every morning for a year.

choices.text: Pretend not to notice, once

effects.log: You keep your horn still for the flying. The page is so astonished that it takes a week to lie again. Your horn feels slightly dusty for a month.

choices.text: Watch the last one closely

effects.log: On the morning the page says my teacher is kind, your horn does not move, and the page goes very quiet. It was not meant to be true. It was, though.

events.text: The page is older and has learned a harder game: things that are half true. 'The minister was at home that night.' Your horn trembles, and does not know which way to go.
events.arc: The Child Who Lies to Your Horn

choices.text: Tell the page a half-truth is a lie in a hat

effects.log: The page writes it on the inside of a sleeve and does not play the game again for a long time.

choices.text: Let the horn tremble, and learn

effects.log: You let it tremble. You learn from the page what a careful mouth can do, and the page learns what it looks like to a horn.

choices.text: Ask which minister

effects.log: The page goes white, then tells you. Three days later the censors are at the minister's door, and a fire that had been waiting under that roof never comes.

events.text: The page is a censor now, in blue robes, with a censor's hat embroidered with your face. On the first morning in office the censor stops at your gate as of old, and says: I will never lie to the king. Then waits.
events.arc: The Child Who Lies to Your Horn

choices.text: Hold your horn still

effects.log: It is true, on the day it is said. You both know the hard part is every day after.

choices.text: Dip it, just a little

effects.log: The censor laughs, then does not. 'Not never,' the censor says. 'Rarely.' Your horn rises.

events.text: A minister has paid for a pair of stone haechi to stand before his own mansion gate: your likeness, life size, very fine. Since they went up, nobody in the ward dares accuse him of anything, because the haechi at his gate would surely have noticed. You notice. He takes a cut of the salt tax.

choices.text: Lie before his gate a day, horn lowered

effects.log: You leave the palace gate for one day and lie down between your two stone likenesses with your horn pointed at the door. The ward understands at once.

choices.text: Lend the statues a sliver of your sight

effects.log: You lend the stone eyes a sliver of your sight. After that the minister's own servants cannot walk past them with a lie, and the salt ledgers leak out of the house one page at a time.

choices.text: Leave it to the censors

effects.log: The censors do not come. The salt tax keeps thinning, and you lie at the palace gate with a taste of salt in your mouth all winter.

events.text: The minister has gone. The mansion is a school for clerks now, and the stone haechi still stand at its gate. The clerks' children climb on them, and one has chipped the horn of the left one with a stone.

choices.text: Let the chipped horn be

effects.log: A chipped horn on a stone haechi is still a horn. The children are frightened of it for a week and then fond of it for ever.

choices.text: Lie by the school gate one night

effects.log: The children see the real horn in the moonlight, unchipped, and the left statue is never climbed again. They climb the right one twice as much.

choices.text: Have the clerks swear their oaths before the chipped one

effects.log: The school takes it up: every new clerk swears before the broken horn. An honest clerk, they say, is one who can.

events.text: The sliver of sight you lent the stone has never come back. Some nights, lying at the palace gate, you see through the stone at the school: a ledger altered, a clerk asleep on duty, a child crying behind the woodpile.

choices.text: Call the sliver home

effects.log: It comes back like a cold drop of water in the eye. You see the Fire Mountain clearer than you have in years, and the school is only a school again.

choices.text: Leave it there, and keep watching

effects.log: You leave it. The altered ledger is found by morning, somehow. The school's clerks are the most honest in the capital, and your own sight is a little dimmer.

choices.text: Look at the crying child first

effects.log: You send a dream to the school's cook, who finds the child behind the woodpile and feeds it, and the child grows up to cook there too.

events.text: {npc}, stooped and old, with a cane, comes to your gate at dawn and kneels. Forty years ago {he} stood here and swore a neighbour had stolen a field-stone; your horn dipped at {him}, not the neighbour, and {he} went to the stocks. {He} has come to say {he} has been angry with you every day since, and would like to stop.

choices.text: Lower your head to {him}, gently

effects.log: {npc} puts a hand flat on your horn, the way one touches a hot pot, and then leaves it there. Neither of you is angry by the time the gate opens.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} lied

effects.log: {npc} tells you. The neighbour was given the field {npc} had been promised. It is not a reason. It is the truth, and your horn is quiet for it.

choices.text: Stay still: forgiving is not the horn's work

effects.log: You stay still. {npc} waits a long time, then nods, as if that were an answer, and goes home lighter anyway.

events.text: {npc} comes back with the neighbour, who is even older and carried in a chair. They have not spoken in forty years. They would like you to settle, at last, who owns the field-stone. It is in a cart behind them, wrapped in straw.

choices.text: Touch your horn to the stone

effects.log: You touch the stone with your horn. It is only a stone. It belongs to nobody. {npc} and the neighbour look at each other and begin, helplessly, to laugh.

choices.text: Ask each of them who it belongs to

effects.log: Both say: the other. Your horn stays still for both. {npc} sits down on the stone and cries for a while, which you allow.

choices.text: Tell them to set it between their houses

effects.log: They set it in the lane between the two houses. It is the most argued-over stone in the ward, and then the most sat-upon.

events.text: {npc} sends a grandchild to your gate with a message. The field-stone is a bench in the lane now, and both families sit on it in the evenings, and it is the most comfortable stone in the ward. {npc} would like you to come and sit by it once.

choices.text: Go, at night

effects.log: You leave the gate for one hour, which you almost never do, and lie down beside the bench in the lane. {npc} sits on it and talks about the weather for the whole hour.

choices.text: Send word that you are sitting by it from here

effects.log: {npc} laughs when the grandchild brings the answer, and says it is exactly what the horn would say.

events.text: An old court musician climbs your ridge with a bamboo flute wrapped in silk. It is the flute of the royal ancestral rite, four hundred years old, and its fifth note has gone flat: a crack nobody can find. Without the fifth note the rite is not the rite. The musician asks if you would sing the note, once, so it can be found again.
events.arc: The Flute That Lost a Note

choices.text: Sing the fifth note

effects.log: You sing it once. The musician plays the flute against it, finds the crack by the sound alone, and binds it with silk thread before the echo is gone.

choices.text: Sing all five, slowly

effects.log: You sing all five. The musician sits down on the ridge and weeps, and gets lost twice going home, and the flute is right again.

choices.text: Sing it with your mate

effects.log: Two voices, one note. The flute's crack closes by itself in the musician's hands, which the musician will never be able to explain to anyone.

events.text: The rite is sung again in the capital, and the court has decided your note was an omen of favour. A minister proposes that the fifth note be played only by order of the throne, and that village musicians be fined for playing it on lesser flutes.
events.arc: The Flute That Lost a Note

choices.text: Sing the fifth note over every village in the province

effects.log: You fly the province for a season, singing. By autumn every herd-child with a willow whistle has the note, and the fine cannot be collected.

choices.text: Stay on your ridge: it is not your law

effects.log: You stay where you are. The proposal passes, is never enforced, and is quietly forgotten in a reign or two.

choices.text: Sing it under the minister's window

effects.log: The minister hums it for days without knowing why, and one morning, humming, drops the proposal in the brazier.

events.text: The old musician's apprentice brings you the flute again, properly mended now, and plays you the rite. It is not quite right. It is better than right: the apprentice has put a little of a cowherd's tune in the fifth note.
events.arc: The Flute That Lost a Note

choices.text: Sing the new note back

effects.log: You sing it back with the cowherd in it. The apprentice laughs out loud, which is not done at a rite, and is never sorry.

choices.text: Sing the old one, once, so it is not lost

effects.log: You sing the old note once, clean. The apprentice plays both, one after the other, and teaches both, and the court never notices there are two.

events.text: In the old custom a family plants a paulownia when a child is born and cuts it for a wedding chest when the child marries. The paulownia you sleep in was planted for a farmer's child, and the child is marrying in the spring. The farmer stands at the foot of your tree with an axe and a face full of apology.
events.arc: The Paulownia for the Wedding Chest

choices.text: Fly to another paulownia

effects.log: You go to a tree two ridges over. Your tree is cut the next morning, and the chest made of it is the finest the valley has seen.

choices.text: Sing to the farmer from the branch

effects.log: The farmer listens with the axe on one shoulder until the song ends, then goes home, plants another sapling, and says the wedding chest can be of pine.

choices.text: Drop one feather into the farmer's hands, and go

effects.log: The feather goes into the chest, under the bride's quilts. The tree is cut. A feather of yours is a heavy thing to give a farmhouse, and you feel the weight of it.

events.text: The wedding chest of paulownia wood sits in a farmhouse two valleys over. You can hear it from your new tree: the wood sings a little when the lid is opened, the way the tree sang in the wind.
events.arc: The Paulownia for the Wedding Chest

choices.text: Visit the chest

effects.log: You sit on the farmhouse ridge for an evening. Inside, the lid opens and closes, opens and closes, a bride trying to decide what to keep in it.

choices.text: Let it sing on its own

effects.log: You let it be. It is a chest now, not a tree, and it has its own song.

events.text: The chest has come back up the valley. The bride, old now, has carried it on a frame to plant a paulownia sapling where your tree stood, and has opened the lid on the hillside to air it. Inside, among the quilts, the wood still smells of your branch.
events.arc: The Paulownia for the Wedding Chest

choices.text: Settle on the sapling, though it bends

effects.log: It bends almost to the grass under you, and holds. The old bride claps both hands and sits down on the chest to watch.

choices.text: Sing over the hillside

effects.log: You sing from the air, all five notes. The sapling grows a hand that summer, which saplings do not.

choices.text: Watch from the old stump

effects.log: You perch on the stump of your old tree and watch the sapling go in. Some homes come back by being given up.

events.text: A governor eager for promotion has sent the throne a phoenix: a golden pheasant with its tail dyed five colours and its comb gilded, in a lacquered cage. The court has declared a festival. The pheasant, as far as you can tell from the eaves, is miserable and has dye in its eyes.

choices.text: Come down and sit beside the cage in full sight

effects.log: The court looks from the cage to you and back. Nobody needs to say anything. That night the cage door is quietly left open.

choices.text: Wait for night and sing to the pheasant

effects.log: You sing very low from the eaves. The pheasant stops shivering, and at dawn it is gone from the cage, though nobody saw how.

choices.text: Stay away: your coming is no answer

effects.log: You stay away. The festival is held, the governor is promoted, and the pheasant lives in its cage for a year, then dies of the dye.

events.text: The pheasant has followed your song to the ridge, dye half washed out, and roosts under your paulownia. It cannot go back to the wild with a gilded comb. Every hawk in the province can see it coming.

choices.text: Let it roost under you

effects.log: It roosts under you all winter. The hawks look at it, and then at you, and decide to hunt elsewhere.

choices.text: Lead it to the bamboo groves

effects.log: You lead it to the old bamboo, where the rain is soft and the stalks rub the gilt away. By spring it is a pheasant again.

choices.text: Ask the small birds to hide it

effects.log: The wrens and buntings close round it like a hedge. It spends a year as the most closely guarded pheasant in the land.

events.text: The pheasant is brown and gold again, entirely ordinary, with a family of its own in the millet below your ridge. Every spring its chicks come up the hill in a line and stand under your tree, as if they had been told something about it.

choices.text: Sing for them

effects.log: You sing for the chicks. They listen with their heads on one side and then go back to the millet, very pleased with themselves.

choices.text: Let them stand there

effects.log: They stand a while and go. Every spring they come back. It is a small rite, and it is theirs.

events.text: You are hurrying down the mountain toward a birth: a child of great promise, you are sure of it, with the first cry due at dusk in a village three valleys away. On the only path through the gorge an ant column is crossing, ten thousand strong, carrying their eggs from a flooded nest. It will take them until night.
events.arc: The Ants on the Road to the Birth

choices.text: Wait for the ants

effects.log: You wait. You arrive after the first cry. The child is well. You stand at the gate anyway, late, and the family say a qilin that comes late is still a qilin.

choices.text: Go round by the ridge

effects.log: The ridge is three times as long and full of brambles. You arrive scratched and in time, with burrs in your mane.

choices.text: Ask the ants to let you pass

effects.log: The ants part round your hooves like water round a stone and close behind you. Not one is stepped on, and afterwards you are not sure who did what for whom.

events.text: The child you went down the mountain for is grown, and has become a famous builder of bridges. Every bridge has, at one end, a narrow lane cut in the stone to one side, a hand wide, for ants. Nobody in the county knows why.
events.arc: The Ants on the Road to the Birth

choices.text: Walk the first bridge at dawn

effects.log: You cross it before anyone is up. It is a good bridge. The ant lane is busy.

choices.text: Stand at the far end and be seen

effects.log: The builder sees you from the scaffolding of the next bridge and nearly falls off it, and finishes that bridge faster than any before.

choices.text: Keep out of sight

effects.log: You leave the builder to the bridges. Some things are better done without a qilin watching.

events.text: The bridge-builder is very old now, and lies in the house by the first bridge. In the gorge below, the ant column is crossing again, the hundredth generation of it, along the narrow lane.
events.arc: The Ants on the Road to the Birth

choices.text: Cross the bridge to the house

effects.log: The builder sees you at the door and asks, first thing, whether the ants are using the lane. They are. The builder is satisfied.

choices.text: Wait for the ants first, as before

effects.log: You wait for the ants. This time you are early anyway, and you stand at the door while the builder sleeps, and nothing in the gorge is hurried.

events.text: A hunter, {npc}, has tracked you for three years across four mountains. Not to kill: {he} has broken {his} bow over a knee at the cave mouth to show you, and only wants to see you once, in daylight, so that {his} children will believe {him}.
events.arc: The Hunter Who Broke a Bow

choices.text: Step into the light

effects.log: You step out onto the flat stone. {npc} sits down in the snow and laughs and cries at the same time, and goes home without a single thing to prove it.

choices.text: Leave a hoofprint where {he} sleeps

effects.log: {npc} wakes beside a hoofprint pressed into bare rock, still warm. It is enough. The children believe the rock.

choices.text: Stay hidden: this is a hard age

effects.log: You stay in the dark of the cave. {npc} waits a month and then goes, and you are sorry, and it was right.

events.text: {npc} has become a guide. Hunters who come to the mountain hire {him}, and {he} leads them for days through the best game country without ever finding any game at all. {He} is the worst-paid guide in the province, and very cheerful.
events.arc: The Hunter Who Broke a Bow

choices.text: Walk the deer away ahead of {his} parties

effects.log: You move ahead of every party like a wind, and the deer move with you. {npc} points out tracks all day and sighs that they are always a day old.

choices.text: Let one party see you

effects.log: You let a party of five see you on the far ridge, once. Four of them never hunt again. The fifth becomes a painter. {npc} is very pleased.

events.text: {npc} is old, and has carved a new bow, a small one, for a grandchild. {He} brings it to the cave mouth and asks whether {he} should give it.
events.arc: The Hunter Who Broke a Bow

choices.text: Breathe on the bow

effects.log: You breathe on it once. The grandchild becomes the finest archer of straw targets in the province and never once hits a living thing.

choices.text: Bow your head to the child, not the bow

effects.log: {npc} understands, and brings the grandchild next time instead of the bow. The bow ends up holding beans on a string in the kitchen.

choices.text: Turn back into the cave

effects.log: {npc} understands that too. The bow goes on the wall, uncarried, and the grandchild grows up to keep bees.

events.text: At the autumn festival of a valley town the children make a qilin out of a winnowing basket, two poles and every coloured rag in town, and dance it through the streets: four children inside it and one at the back for the tail. It is the worst qilin you have ever seen. It has three horns.

choices.text: Dance beside it, at the edge of the lantern light

effects.log: Half the town sees two qilin that night, one of them with three horns. The town argues for a year about which was real.

choices.text: Watch from the roofs

effects.log: You watch from a ridge tile until the last lantern goes out. Nobody sees you. You are happy all winter.

choices.text: Lend it one true step

effects.log: Where the basket qilin steps, for one step, the grass flattened by the crowd stands up again. One child notices, and never forgets.

events.text: The children's qilin has become the town's dance, and the town is famous for it. Rival towns now dance rival qilin, larger and finer, and this year two of them meet in a narrow street, their tails tangle, and the dancers inside start pushing.

choices.text: Walk between them

effects.log: The street goes silent. Both qilin bow to you, which is very hard for a basket, and the tails come apart on their own.

choices.text: Untangle the tails with your horn

effects.log: You lift the knot with the tip of your horn as gently as a hair out of rice. Both towns claim the knot was theirs.

choices.text: Let them sort it out

effects.log: They sort it out with a great deal of shouting and no harm. The two tails are kept tangled ever after, and the towns dance together.

events.text: The three-horned basket qilin hangs in the town shrine now, faded and patched, and the first child who danced in it is the oldest person in town. Every festival they carry it out and tie one new rag to it.

choices.text: Leave a hair of your mane in its tail

effects.log: The next morning there is a single gold hair tied among the rags, and nobody can say who tied it. The oldest dancer can, and does not.

choices.text: Come to the festival one last time

effects.log: You walk beside it down the whole street in the lantern light. The oldest dancer walks the other side. Nobody pushes.

events.text: Two people of the village under your mountain have been in love for eleven years, and neither has said a word. The whole village knows. In desperation the village has left a cup of wine and a written request at your shrine: Mountain Spirit, please do something.
events.arc: The Fox Who Was Asked to Matchmake

choices.text: Borrow a face and carry a message

effects.log: As somebody's visiting aunt you deliver a bundle of persimmons to each of them, and say it is from the other. It is not. By spring it does not matter.

choices.text: Send them both the same dream

effects.log: They dream the same dream on the same night, of a well and a bucket and a rope too short. In the morning they meet at the real well, very red.

choices.text: Lead them both astray on the hill

effects.log: Foxfire takes each of them off the path at dusk, by different ways, to the same flat rock. They sit there until the moon is up, talking about foxes.

events.text: The wedding is in the spring, and the village insists the mountain spirit be given the seat of honour. There is a cushion left empty at the head of the table, with a cup of wine before it, and every guest bows to it.
events.arc: The Fox Who Was Asked to Matchmake

choices.text: Come in a borrowed face and sit on the cushion

effects.log: Nobody can remember afterwards who sat at the head of the table. Everybody agrees it was a very good guest.

choices.text: Come as a fox, under the table

effects.log: Somebody's child finds you under the table and sits there with you for the whole feast, very solemn, and tells nobody.

choices.text: Stay on the mountain and listen

effects.log: You lie on the mound and listen to the drums. The bead in your mouth is warm all night.

events.text: The village has decided the mountain spirit is a matchmaker. There are nine requests at your shrine now, including one from a widower of eighty for the widow next door, and one, in a child's hand, on behalf of a dog.
events.arc: The Fox Who Was Asked to Matchmake

choices.text: Take the widower's case

effects.log: It takes a winter of foxfire and borrowed aunts. The widow says yes on the condition that he stops pretending to be deaf. He says what.

choices.text: Take the dog's case

effects.log: The dog is matched with the dog at the mill. The child is satisfied. The miller is not, but comes round.

choices.text: Turn the requests back with a gust

effects.log: A gust takes all nine papers off the shrine and drops them on nine doorsteps. The village takes this as a reply and gets on with it alone.

events.text: {npc}, very old, on a stick, stops you in a market lane and stares at your borrowed face. Sixty years ago {he} shared a room with that face in a scholars' lodging, and the face has not changed by a line. {He} does not shout. {He} only says: 'I always knew there was something.'

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth

effects.log: {npc} listens to all of it on a bench by the salt stall and says, at the end, 'You still owe me a pair of socks.'

choices.text: Say you are the old friend's grandchild

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, does not believe a word, and walks with you to the end of the lane anyway.

choices.text: Slip away into the crowd

effects.log: You are gone between one step and the next. Behind you {npc} calls the old name, once.

events.text: {npc} has taken to climbing the hill to your grave mound every tenth day, very slowly, with a cushion, to talk about the old lodging: the landlord's goose, the examination you both failed, the night the roof leaked onto the classics.

choices.text: Listen in your own fur

effects.log: You lie on the mound as a fox and {npc} talks to you as if it were the most natural thing in the world. Perhaps it is.

choices.text: Wear the old face for {him}

effects.log: You put on the old face. {npc} says it is like being young for an afternoon, and then goes home and sleeps for two days.

choices.text: Come down the hill to {him} instead

effects.log: You meet {npc} at the bottom of the hill from then on, and walk, and the village starts to talk about the old scholar's young friend.

events.text: {npc} is failing. On the last climb {he} asks, out of breath, whether a fox can give a person a little more time.

choices.text: Lend {him} a breath of the bead

effects.log: You breathe a little of the bead into {npc}. The next morning {npc} walks to the market alone, buys the socks, and leaves them on your mound.

choices.text: Say no, and stay with {him}

effects.log: You say no. {npc} nods, and says that was the right answer, and you sit together until the sun is off the mound.

choices.text: Say nothing, and hold {his} hand

effects.log: You take {npc}'s hand in a hand you borrowed long ago. It is answer enough for both of you.

events.text: A young fox with two tails and no manners has moved onto the grave mounds on your hill, and on full-moon nights it creeps down to the village and borrows breaths from sleeping children, the quick way, the way you remember. It has heard of you, and thinks you are a story for kits.
events.arc: The Young Fox on Your Mound

choices.text: Show it all your tails

effects.log: You open every tail at once on the ridge. The young fox lies flat in the grass for an hour. The village sees a glow on the hill and talks of nothing else.

choices.text: Teach it to bow to the moon instead

effects.log: It bows badly and complains the whole time, but it bows.

choices.text: Give the children's breath back yourself

effects.log: You go down to the village on the next full moon and breathe a little of your own bead into every child the young fox visited. The children sleep late.

events.text: The young fox has three tails now, and has come to complain. The moon way is slow. It has bowed for eight years and the bead in its mouth is the size of a lentil. Yours, it points out, is the size of a plum. How many breaths did you borrow?
events.arc: The Young Fox on Your Mound

choices.text: Tell it the truth

effects.log: You tell it the number. It is quiet for a long time, and then goes back to bowing, slower and more seriously than before.

choices.text: Tell it none

effects.log: It knows a lie when it hears one: foxes do. It goes back to bowing, angrier, and does not visit for a century.

choices.text: Lend it a little of your bead

effects.log: You breathe a little of your bead into it. Its lentil is a pea now. It is so pleased it forgets to complain for a whole year.

events.text: A four-tailed fox stands at the edge of your mound one autumn with a kit behind it, a red-brown scrap of a thing, blind and then not. It has come to ask you to tell the kit about the moon.
events.arc: The Young Fox on Your Mound

choices.text: Tell the kit

effects.log: You tell the kit about the moon, and the mounds, and the slow way. The kit falls asleep in the middle, which is how it should be.

choices.text: Let the four-tailed fox tell it, and listen

effects.log: It tells it differently from you. Better, in places. You do not say so, but your tails do.

events.text: In a farmhouse of the south the kitchen fire has refused to light for three days. Tomorrow is the rite for the grandfather of the house, and there is no rice cooked, no soup, nothing for the ancestral table. The widow of the house has blown on the kindling until she is dizzy. A swallow brings you the news, with a complaint about the weather.
events.arc: The Kitchen That Would Not Light

choices.text: Go yourself, and light it

effects.log: You come down the flue like a red leaf. The kindling catches with a sound like someone saying oh. The widow sits down on the kitchen floor and laughs.

choices.text: Find out why it will not light

effects.log: You find the kitchen god of the house sitting in the flue in a sulk: nobody has thanked it since the old man died. You talk it down, and the fire lights.

choices.text: Send a spark with the swallow

effects.log: The swallow drops the spark in the woodshed. The woodshed lights beautifully. The kitchen lights from the woodshed. The widow is no longer dizzy, only very busy.

events.text: The fire in that kitchen has not gone out since. The widow's grandson cooks on it now, and talks to it while cooking, telling it the village gossip, and the fire, you notice, burns warmer for good gossip.
events.arc: The Kitchen That Would Not Light

choices.text: Send it better gossip by the swallows

effects.log: The swallows bring the kitchen news from every eave in the south. The grandson's soup becomes famous, and so, unaccountably, does the grandson.

choices.text: Teach the fire to keep a secret

effects.log: The fire learns to hear a secret and not flare at it. The grandson tells it everything and the village never finds out.

choices.text: Sit on the roof and listen yourself

effects.log: You sit on the ridge-pole through a whole winter of gossip. It is the warmest winter you have had in a century.

events.text: The farmhouse is sold, and the family carry the fire to their new house in a clay jar on a carrying pole, three days' walk, feeding it pine cones on the road. On the second night it rains.
events.arc: The Kitchen That Would Not Light

choices.text: Fly over the jar and keep the rain off

effects.log: You hang over the road all night with your wings spread. The rain steams off you. The jar is dry, and you are very tired.

choices.text: Trust the family

effects.log: The grandson takes off a coat and holds it over the jar all night, and the fire comes through the rain coughing, and lives.

choices.text: Wait at the new house, ready

effects.log: The fire comes in weak. You are in the new hearth when it arrives, and the two of you make one good fire between you.

events.text: A workshop of the southern garrison makes fire-arrows: tubes of black powder strapped to arrow shafts, a hundred to a cart, that scream as they fly. The master of the workshop has climbed to the hill you face to ask for your fire, for the fuses, so they will never fail in rain.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: The master goes down the hill with damp fuses and a sour face. You watch the garrison all year, and nothing screams.

choices.text: Give it, for the coast's defence

effects.log: The fuses never fail again. You can feel every arrow they fire, from a hundred li, like a scratch on your own skin.

choices.text: Give it for New Year instead

effects.log: You give your fire on one condition: once a year the workshop fires its arrows straight up over the town at New Year, unloaded, for nothing but light.

events.text: Raiders on the coast at dawn, forty sails. From your hill you feel every fuse take your fire, one after another, and the arrows go up screaming. You could still pull the fire back.

choices.text: Let the arrows fly

effects.log: The raiders turn back with their sails alight. You are a long time cooling afterwards, and the swallows avoid you for a season.

choices.text: Pull the fire from the sails, not from the sky

effects.log: The arrows scream over the ships and burst over the sea like red flowers. The raiders take fright anyway, and nobody aboard is burned.

events.text: The New Year sky over the garrison town is full of screaming red light, and the town loves it. The children make small fire-arrows of their own from paper and pilfered powder, and this year one has set a thatched roof alight.

choices.text: Call the fire out of the thatch

effects.log: You call it and it comes, out of the thatch and up to you like a dog to a whistle. The roof is scorched and the children are very quiet.

choices.text: Let the town put it out, and learn

effects.log: The town puts it out with buckets and shouting. Next year the children's arrows are fired from the riverbank, by order.

events.text: The garrison is long gone, but the town still fires arrows straight up at New Year, unloaded, and calls them the Bird's Feathers. An old powder-maker climbs your hill with the last of the original fuses, wrapped in oiled paper.

choices.text: Light it one more time

effects.log: You touch it. It goes up alone over the dark town, screaming, and bursts into a red bird for a breath. The town says that one was yours. It was.

choices.text: Keep it unlit

effects.log: You keep the fuse unlit in the eaves. The powder-maker says that is the best place for it.

events.text: A mountain village in the north has lost every fire in a single night of storm. A child of eleven was sent down to the next village for an ember and is climbing back up through the snow at dusk with it in a clay pot, blowing on it, and the ember is dying.

choices.text: Fly down and settle on the pot

effects.log: You settle on the pot like a hen on an egg. It warms in the child's hands, and the child climbs the rest of the way without once looking up.

choices.text: Fly ahead and light the village yourself

effects.log: The child arrives to find every hearth already burning and is furious about it for years.

choices.text: Breathe once into the pot from the air

effects.log: The ember brightens. The child never sees you, and tells the story all life long as a story about good blowing.

events.text: The child who carried the ember up the mountain is the village's fire-keeper now, and the village has a custom: the first fire of each winter is carried up from the valley in a clay pot, by the youngest who can make the climb. This year it is snowing again.

choices.text: Fly above the climbers

effects.log: You fly above the line of climbers all the way up, too high to be seen, low enough to be warm.

choices.text: Let them do it alone

effects.log: They do it alone. The ember arrives faint and alive, and the village cheers for a child who did it without help.

choices.text: Put a little of yourself into the ember

effects.log: The ember arrives burning red and bright. It will not go out in that village for a long time.

events.text: The fire-keeper is old, and climbs the mountain one last time behind the youngest carrier. At the top the old keeper asks the child to stop and turn round, and look at the sky, where a red bird is circling over the snow.

choices.text: Circle lower

effects.log: You come down low enough for the child to see your crest. The old keeper says nothing at all, only nods, as if a debt had been paid in the right coin.

choices.text: Light the snow red for a moment

effects.log: For one breath the whole snowfield glows red, and then is white again. The child will carry the ember up for the rest of a long life.

events.text: You know every foot that crosses the palace above you: the slippers of the eunuchs, the boots of the guard, the king's slow heels. One pair of boots has walked the same small circle in the east courtyard every night for a month, round a single paving stone, from the second watch to dawn. It is {npc}, a guard. Through the stone you can feel {he} is grieving.

choices.text: Warm the paving stone under {his} feet

effects.log: {npc} stops walking, puts a hand on the warm stone, and sits down on it until dawn.

choices.text: Hum through the stone

effects.log: A low hum comes up through the paving, too low for the ear, felt in the bones. {npc} stands still and listens, and the circle stops.

choices.text: Let {him} walk: grief must walk

effects.log: You let {npc} walk. By the end of the season the circle is smaller, and then it is gone.

events.text: {npc} has put a small cup of water on the warm paving stone every night since, and talks to it. You learn the whole story without moving: a child, a fever, a winter in the guards' quarters with no fuel. And you learn the quarters are cold because the fuel ration is sold before it reaches them.

choices.text: Jam the storehouse door with a settling of the ground

effects.log: The ground under the storehouse settles a finger's breadth. The quartermaster's cart sticks in the door at midnight, full of fuel, in front of the whole watch.

choices.text: Warm the floor of the guards' quarters all winter

effects.log: You warm the floor of the quarters like a heated room through the whole winter. Nobody there is sick that year.

choices.text: Tell the king in a dream

effects.log: The king dreams of a cold room full of coughing and wakes asking for the fuel ledgers.

events.text: {npc} is captain of the gate now, and on the first night of every winter goes to the east courtyard and stands on the paving stone a while. Lately {he} has been bringing the youngest guards, one at a time, and saying nothing.

choices.text: Warm the stone for each of them

effects.log: Each young guard feels it: a warmth under the boots, like a hand. Each one looks at {npc}, and {npc} only nods.

choices.text: Keep the stone cold, and let {npc} be the warm thing

effects.log: The stone stays cold. {npc} puts a hand on each young shoulder instead. Setting down is part of holding.

events.text: The palace needs a new well, and the geomancers have found the perfect place: the exact centre of the inner courtyard, where the ground is warm in winter and dry in rain. It is, as you could have told them, your spine. The diggers start at dawn.
events.arc: The Well Dug Into Your Back

choices.text: Let them dig, and give them water

effects.log: Three spades deep, then nine. At the twelfth the clay goes soft and warm and the water comes up yellow-clear and sweet. You feel the well in your back like a held breath.

choices.text: Turn the clay as hard as iron

effects.log: The spades ring and bounce. The geomancers decide the centre is sacred, and dig in the kitchen yard instead.

choices.text: Soften the ground one courtyard over

effects.log: The diggers hit water one courtyard east, early and easily, and decide the geomancers were a little out.

events.text: The well in your back is the palace's favourite. The king drinks from it, the cooks swear by it, and the court ladies say its water keeps the skin young. Now a minister wants a second well dug beside it, and a third for the princes.
events.arc: The Well Dug Into Your Back

choices.text: Allow one more

effects.log: The second well goes in a little left of your spine. Two held breaths now. You manage.

choices.text: Let the first well run low for a season

effects.log: The first well drops to a trickle for one summer. The court learns that the centre gives what it gives, and the minister's plan is shelved.

choices.text: Make the water taste of whoever draws it

effects.log: The minister draws a cup and it tastes of old ink and ambition. The proposal is dropped, and the minister drinks tea from then on.

events.text: A siege. The gates are shut, the river is held by the enemy, and the city's wells have been fouled. Only one well in the capital still runs clean, the one in your back, and the king has opened the inner courtyard to the city. The queue runs out of the palace and down the avenue.
events.arc: The Well Dug Into Your Back

choices.text: Give everything the well can give

effects.log: You give until the clay round the well is dry and cracked and your whole length aches. The city drinks for forty days, and the siege breaks before the well does.

choices.text: Give, and keep enough to stay whole

effects.log: You give a steady, careful measure every day. The city is thirsty and alive, and so are you.

events.text: A small prince of five has discovered that if you lie flat on the heated floor of the east hall and press an ear to it, something underneath is breathing. Every afternoon now the prince lies on the floor through lessons, ear down, and the tutor has given up.
events.arc: The Child Who Listens to the Floor

choices.text: Breathe slower, to send the prince to sleep

effects.log: The prince is asleep in a quarter of an hour, every afternoon. The tutor teaches the sleeping child anyway, very softly.

choices.text: Hum the five notes for the prince

effects.log: The prince learns all five notes before learning to write a single character, and hums them for the rest of a long life.

choices.text: Hold your breath

effects.log: The prince is distraught. The tutor is delighted. You last one day, and the breathing comes back, and so does the prince.

events.text: The small prince is the crown prince now, grown and grave, and the court says a crown prince does not lie on floors. He still does, at night, alone, in the east hall. He has started telling the floor about the kingdom: the tax roll, the flood in the south, his father's temper.
events.arc: The Child Who Listens to the Floor

choices.text: Warm the floor where the flood is spoken of

effects.log: The floor is warm under the prince's hand at the word flood, and the prince asks for the southern reports the next morning.

choices.text: Listen, and only listen

effects.log: You listen. The prince talks until the lamp is out. Some things only need to be set down somewhere.

choices.text: Answer, once

effects.log: A single deep breath comes up through the floor at the end. The prince sits up in the dark and laughs out loud, for the first time in years.

events.text: The king is old. The king who was the prince lies down on the floor of the east hall for the last time, ear down, and says: 'I do not know if I was a good king. You heard all of it. Was I?'
events.arc: The Child Who Listens to the Floor

choices.text: Warm the whole floor

effects.log: The whole hall goes warm, wall to wall, like a summer afternoon. The old king lies there smiling until the attendants come with the lamps.

choices.text: Say nothing: it is not yours to say

effects.log: You say nothing. The old king nods into the floor as if that too were an answer, and it was.

choices.text: Breathe once, deep and slow

effects.log: One breath, the same as on the first afternoon. The king laughs, very quietly, the laugh of a child of five.

events.text: The bronze bell of a mountain temple has cracked in a cold snap, and its voice is a cough. The monks cannot have a new one made. The abbot comes to you with an odd request: eat the iron clapper and the iron bands, so the bronze can be recast clean, and leave the bell its bronze.

choices.text: Eat only the iron, very carefully

effects.log: You pick the iron off the bronze like a child picking beans out of rice. The bronze goes to the founder without a scratch.

choices.text: Refuse: a temple's iron is not for eating

effects.log: The abbot bows and goes. The bell is recast with its iron in it, and coughs a little less, and you are oddly proud of it.

choices.text: Eat it, and give them iron from the mountain

effects.log: You eat the bands and the clapper, then gnaw a seam of ore out of the hill behind the temple and leave it at the founder's door.

events.text: The bell is recast, and the monks have put something new in it: a ring in its crown cast as a tiny beast with needles for fur and a trunk. Every time the bell is struck it hums in your belly like a second stomach.

choices.text: Let it hum

effects.log: You let it hum. Morning and evening, every day, something in you is rung like a bell, and the rice in your tail is warm.

choices.text: Hum back

effects.log: You hum back from the hill. The monks swear the bell has an echo now, a low one, from the wrong direction.

events.text: Soldiers come for the bell: the army needs bronze for guns, and every temple bell in the province is to be melted. The abbot, very old now, stands in the bell pavilion with a broom.

choices.text: Eat the soldiers' spearheads

effects.log: You eat every spearhead in the column, one at a time, while the soldiers watch. They go home with poles. The bell stays. The iron sits heavy and taken in your belly.

choices.text: Lie down in front of the pavilion

effects.log: An iron hill lies down in front of a bell. The soldiers look at you for a long time and go away to write a report. It is never answered.

choices.text: Let the bell go

effects.log: You let it go. The abbot puts the broom away. In the spring, from a hill far away, you hear a gun fire, and something in your belly hums once.

events.text: An old seamstress who has sewn for the village for sixty years lays her last needle on your trunk. Her eyes are gone; she can no longer thread it. It is the only iron she owns. She says she would rather it was eaten by you than lost in a crack in the floor.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: It is the smallest thing you have eaten in centuries, and you taste sixty years of hems in it.

choices.text: Thread it for her with your trunk

effects.log: It takes all afternoon and a great deal of breathing. When the thread goes through, the seamstress laughs and sews you a single stitch in the air.

choices.text: Keep it in your fur, uneaten

effects.log: You tuck it among the needles on your back. Of ten thousand iron needles there, one is not yours.

events.text: The seamstress has died, and the village has asked you to the funeral, which is a first for the village and very nearly for you. They have left a space at the edge of the yard the size of a small hill.

choices.text: Go, and stand at the edge

effects.log: You stand in the space they left. The mourners look at you and then do not, which is the kindest thing a village can do.

choices.text: Go, and lay the needle on the coffin

effects.log: You lay the needle on the coffin lid with your trunk. The village keeps it in the shrine after, the needle the Iron-Eater gave back.

choices.text: Stay on your hill

effects.log: You stay where you are and listen to the drums come up the valley. The rice in your tail is heavy all day.

events.text: The seamstress's great-granddaughter is a seamstress too, and comes up the hill with her own first commission: a coat for you. It is made of forty bolts of hemp and does not fit.

choices.text: Wear it

effects.log: It lasts one winter before the needles come through, and the village says you look like a haystack in mourning.

choices.text: Let her measure you properly

effects.log: She measures you for nine days with a knotted rope and a ladder. The second coat fits. Mostly.

choices.text: Lie down so she can see all of you

effects.log: You lie down on the hillside. She walks round you twice, then sits down on your tail and laughs until she cries, and starts again on paper.

events.text: The children of the village under your hill have made a game of you. They hunt the lanes for rusty nails, bent hinges and old horseshoes and bring them up the hill in a basket, and the child with the most iron gets to ride your back down the slope.

choices.text: Eat it all, and give the rides

effects.log: You eat every nail and give every ride. The slope is worn into a groove by the end of summer.

choices.text: Give the rides, and leave the iron for the smith

effects.log: The rides are free. The basket goes down to the smith every evening. The smith is pleased, and slightly suspicious.

choices.text: Eat only the rust

effects.log: You lick the rust off every nail and hand them back shining. The children think this is the best trick they have ever seen.

events.text: The village smith climbs the hill, sooty to the elbows and furious. The children have started prising nails out of fences. Three fences have fallen down, and a gate, and the smith's own horseshoes are missing from the forge.

choices.text: Give back the smith's horseshoes

effects.log: You give back what is left of the horseshoes, which is not much. The smith takes them and, somehow, laughs.

choices.text: Change the rules: only iron nobody needs

effects.log: You will eat nothing that holds anything up. The children learn the difference between junk and a hinge faster than any apprentice.

choices.text: Pull the fences straight with your trunk

effects.log: You straighten every fence in the village in one night. They are slightly crooked in a new way, which the village decides is your style.

events.text: The children of the nail game are grown. One of them is the village smith now, and keeps a basket by the forge door marked FOR THE HILL: offcuts, spoilt nails, the iron nobody needs. Every new moon the basket is full.

choices.text: Eat from it

effects.log: You come down at the new moon and eat from the basket, and the smith's own children ride you home.

choices.text: Leave it for the next game

effects.log: You leave the basket where it is. By summer the smith's children are carrying it up the hill, and the game begins again.
